create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.text: Create a registry and manage its keys on the proved design.

As Carol, you create a registry for an application with one command and read its address and its state token from the receipt. As Alice, you book the registration of a key with its payload and a deposit, and the receipt names the pending registration the booking made. As Bob, you fold the registrations you name into the registry from the chain alone, and keep what each of them holds above its deposit. As Alice again, when nobody folds your registration you take it back inside its reclaim window, and when that window has passed anyone can clean it up and your deposit goes back to the refund address you chose. When a command is interrupted, the next write of the same wallet settles what it left, and nothing is ever sent a second time.

The first diagram shows the life of one registration. A booking makes it pending. Until its processing deadline only a fold can spend it. After the deadline, and until the reclaim window ends, only the refund address can take it back. After the window anyone can clean it up.

This page describes ten commands: singular registry create, open-datum create, open-datum fold, open-datum insert, open-datum reclaim and open-datum cleanup, open-datum update and open-datum terminate, singular registry inspect and open-datum inspect. Every flag they take is listed with its description and its default in the settings table, and each command prints the same information with --help.

create-a-registry.text: As Carol, you spend one output of your wallet to make a registry, and the output you spend fixes the registry's identity.

The second diagram shows what a creation does. The command reads your wallet and looks for live reference copies of the validators. The first registry of an application publishes each in its own transaction, state first, and waits for both before it creates the registry. If you stop between publications, a rerun finds the live copy and publishes only the missing script. A later registry finds both live copies and sends one transaction. The registry's state token appears on the first output of the creation, and the command reads it back before it prints the receipt.

open-datum create makes a registry of open datum. Five parameters are fixed here for the life of the registry: the processing time and the reclaim time of a booked registration (--process-time and --reclaim-time), the widest validity interval a booking may declare (--booking-width), and the registration cost and the minimum tip (--registration-cost and --minimum-tip), which the registry carries and nothing enforces.

singular registry create makes the registry of any application whose policy you give with --application-policy: the policy is the one parameter of the state validator. The command publishes the state validator when no live copy of it exists, and creates the registry whose state token that validator guards.

The seed is your wallet's largest ada-only output, chosen when the registry is built and after the validators have been published when they had to be, so the publication cannot have spent it. --seed names another output of your wallet. The wallet funds the transactions and keeps their change. The builders choose the funding, so these commands refuse --fund-input, --max-outlay and --preview by name rather than ignore them.

The receipt names the registry's address and fingerprint, its state token, the seed, the output that now holds the state, the registry's root, the policy of the application, each validator with the output that carries its reference script and whether this command published it, and every transaction the command sent with what became of it.

book-a-registration.text: As Alice, you book a key with its payload and a deposit under a registry you name by its address, and the registry's configuration decides the deadlines.

The booking puts a pending registration at the request address of open datum. It holds the deposit (2 000 000 lovelace unless --deposit says more; a deposit below the minimum ADA of the output that will hold the key's token with its payload is refused, naming that minimum), the tip for whoever folds it (--tip, nothing by default), and its approval, the token that a fold, a reclaim or a cleanup consumes. The payload is the file --payload names, read in the form --payload-schema gives, plain JSON unless you say otherwise; store ordinary JSON as a key's payload gives the rules. --refund-address says where a reclaim or a cleanup returns the value, and it is your own address when you do not say.

The receipt names the pending registration, its approval, the key, the deposit, the tip, the refund address and the three times that matter: when it was booked, its processing deadline, and the end of its reclaim window. Whoever folds it, or you taking it back, names the pending registration with --pending.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: Fold registrations and terminations into the registry.
As Bob, you fold the registrations you name into the registry in one transaction, and you need nothing from anyone who booked them.

Each registration's approval is consumed and the key's token is minted into the holding the registration committed to. The fold is built from the chain alone, and the wallet that runs it keeps what each request holds above its deposit. Nothing is chosen for you: every registration is named with --pending, and a registration that cannot be folded refuses the command, saying why.
The receipt names the registry's new root, the output that holds the state, and each registration folded with its key.

where-the-keys-token-goes.text: A registration commits, when it is booked, to the address that will hold its key's token once it is folded. open-datum insert commits the request address of open datum. The fold accepts any address a registration committed to, the address of the state validator itself included. A token folded into a holding at the state validator's own address stays where only the state validator can spend it. That is the choice of whoever booked the registration, and the fold does not refuse it.

update-a-live-holding.text: As Alice, you choose the output that holds your active key and replace its payload. The control stays the same: its registry, active token, key, controller and protected deposit. The holding keeps all its tokens and at least the deposit. If the larger datum needs more minimum ADA, your wallet supplies it. No registry state is spent by the update.

The receipt names the new holding output. Use that reference for a later update or termination. A missing holding, another controller, or another named registry is refused before the transaction is signed.

book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.text: Book permanent termination, then fold it.

As Alice, you choose your live holding and book permanent termination. Its protected deposit is donated to the treasury in this transaction. The new request has no datum and holds exactly the active token and one termination approval; its ADA is the reward available to the folder. The active token moves into this request and is not burned at booking. There is no reclaim or cancellation window for this booking.

The receipt names the pending output and the treasuryDonation in lovelace. As Bob, you fold that pending output with open-datum fold, using --pending TXID#IX and your own vault. You need the public chain and your wallet; Alice's key, local directory and records are unnecessary. The fold burns the active token and the approval, creates no replacement holding, and leaves the key terminal permanently. You receive the request's whole value; your ordinary wallet input pays the transaction fee. A batch may mix terminations with registrations of other keys. A termination has no processing deadline.

take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.text: Take a registration back, or clean it up.
As Alice, you take back a registration you booked while its reclaim window is open.

Everything the registration holds returns to its refund address, which must be the wallet that runs the command, and its approval is burned. Before the window opens or after it closes the command is refused, saying when.
As anyone, you clean up an expired registration once its reclaim window has ended.

The deposit returns to the refund address, the wallet that runs the command keeps what the request holds above the deposit, and the approval is burned. Both commands name exactly one pending registration.

when-a-command-is-interrupted.text: As any of the three, you may lose the connection, stop the command, or run past --confirm-timeout. The command never sends a transaction twice.

The third diagram shows what happens to a transaction that was in flight. Every transaction is written to the journal under its identity before it is sent. If the command is interrupted, whatever the moment, the transaction keeps that identity. The next write of the same wallet for the same registry reads its journal before it builds anything. A transaction the chain holds is recorded as landed and named under reconciled in the next receipt, and a transaction the node refused stays recorded as refused. A transaction the chain does not yet show stops the next write, naming it, and nothing is built or sent until it is settled. A creation is journalled under the application and the wallet, because the name of the registry it makes is known only once its seed is chosen; the other commands are journalled under the registry.
--state-dir names the root of the journals, and the default is the per-user state directory. Recovering a registry command shows each of these interruptions on a development network.

read-a-key.text: As a reader, give the registry address and a key to either inspect command. No signer, blueprint or local state directory is needed.

The neutral command identifies the application from the packaged release table and answers active, terminal or never registered, or reports an unavailable read or a refusal with its reason. Active custody includes its datum as data. The application command decodes a live holding's protected control, deposit and payload, or identifies pending termination. Both retain the authenticated state requirement for absence and every neutral refusal.

Human text is the default; --json selects one JSON object. --query-work adds measured calls, rows and bytes per provider read and in total. Answers exit 0, unavailable reads exit 1, and refused evidence or invalid command lines exit 2. See reading a key for settings, classification order, refusal reasons and measurement limits.
